sources.text:
Deadly Apache Helicopter crash highlights growing Central Texas fire risk
AUSTIN, Texas — A deadly helicopter crash near Salado sparked a wildfire Wednesday as crews across Central Texas continued battling elevated fire danger and multiple blazes.
An Apache helicopter went down in a field about 20 miles from Fort Hood, killing two Fort Hood soldiers. Investigators said the helicopter did not hit any people or structures.
“It crashed into a field. You could tell it was a violent crash,” said Cliff Coleman, a public information officer with the Bell County Sheriff’s Office.
The crash sparked the Dove Hollow Fire near Salado. According to the Bell County Sheriff's Office, the fire was fully contained by Thursday afternoon. Five homes were threatened, but all were saved. Only one outbuilding was lost.
"Approximately 155 acres burned. Although that is a significant amount of land, the outcome could have been catastrophic without the large and rapid response from fire departments across Bell County and neighboring counties," the sheriff's office said.
More than 200 firefighters from 22 agencies assisted with the response.
The helicopter crash came as wildfire danger remained elevated across Texas. Reilly Ruggiero, a public information officer with the Texas A&M Forest Service, said crews in the Hill Country and Central Texas have faced “topographic challenges” and “tricky” terrain, but containment has been helped by heavy equipment and aircraft.
“Thankfully, our heavy equipment ground personnel have been able to contain them, and aircraft has helped us suppress this as well,” Ruggiero said.
Overnight, crews continued working to make sure containment lines held and to watch for hotspots and embers, which can be easier to spot in the dark.
"Local and volunteer fire departments will stay on scene of a fire during the nighttime to ensure containment lines hold; higher humidity levels and cooler temperatures during the nighttime allow firefighters to have an advantage on suppression efforts to increase containment,” Ruggiero said.
In Burnet County, the Saxon, Sandy, and Flat Rock fires have been contained, according to the Texas A&M Forest Service map.
Counties across Texas have asked residents not to burn. In Central Texas, burn bans include Travis, Hays, Llano and Burnet counties.
Ruggiero said fine fuels such as grasses can dry quickly even after rain.
“So those are our grasses and very fine fuel types. Even though we did have some significant rain a couple of weeks ago, those types of fuels can dry out extremely fast. So that's what we're looking at, coupled with multiple days of extremely hot temperatures and some gusty winds overall have been increasing our wildfire risk throughout the state,” Ruggiero said.
Questions remained about the helicopter crash:
- Who were the soldiers?
- What caused the crash?
- Where was the helicopter headed?
We will update you here, on social media, and on air as soon as we have those answers.

Two crew members aboard an AH-64E Army Apache helicopter from Fort Hood, Texas, were killed when the aircraft crashed on Wednesday, a Fort Hood news release says.
Both soldiers’ names are being withheld pending next of kin notification, the news release says. The soldiers will be transported to Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center at Fort Hood.
“Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the families, friends, and fellow Troopers of those involved during this incredibly difficult time,” Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general of the 1st Cavalry Division, said in a statement.
Top Stories This Week
The helicopter went down in Salado, Texas — less than 30 miles southeast of the Army base. The two crew members aboard the Apache were pronounced dead at the scene Wednesday afternoon, said Cliff Coleman, a spokesman for the Bell County Sheriff’s Office.
Coleman said the two crew members were the only ones aboard the helicopter at the time of the crash and referred further questions to officials at Fort Hood and the Army’s Criminal Investigation Division.
The Apache crash is the latest military aircraft training accident in recent months. In May, two Navy EA-18G Growler jets collided midair during a demonstration at Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho and all four pilots ejected. In June, a Marine Corps F/A-18 Hornet crashed and a pilot ejected near Mount Rainier in Washington state. Also that month, eight people were killed after an Air Force B-52 Stratofortress crashed after taking off from Edwards Air Force Base in California. Then, just last month, an F-35B crashed while landing at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in Southern California. The pilot was recovered and treated for non-life threatening injuries.

sources.news_title: 2 Killed in Military Helicopter Crash in Texas
sources.text:
Two members of the U.S. military died when a U.S. Army Apache helicopter crashed in Bell County, Texas, on Wednesday.
The aircraft was based out of Fort Hood, near Killeen, and came down in Salado, about 20 miles away.
Fort Hood said the names of the two soldiers who died in the crash would be withheld “until 24 hours after notification of next of kin.” The crash also started a wildfire that required containment.
The wildfire forced several residents of Salado to evacuate their homes, though no building damage has been reported.
Emergency services, military responders, and law enforcement rushed to the scene.
“Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts,” said Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general of the 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, in a statement. “Our thoughts are with the crew and their families.”
Several Texas elected representatives offered condolences as well on their social media accounts, including Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, and Sen. John Cornyn.
Abbott filled followers in on what had happened and asked them to join his wife “Cecilia and me in prayer for their families and the entire Fort Hood community,” adding that “Texas is forever indebted to those who serve our state and nation.”
According to manufacturer Boeing, the Apache AH-64 is “the world’s most advanced, proven attack helicopter” that is used by “19 countries and counting.”
An Apache is typically crewed by two people, has a length and height of 48.2 feet and 15.5 feet, respectively, and weighs a little over 15,000 lbs. when outfitted for most missions. There are currently more than 1,300 of these helicopters in service around the world, and a collective 1.3 million flight hours of combat have been recorded.
Boeing and the U.S. military have worked to improve the helicopter’s nitrogen inerting units and other systems to cut down on the damage an Apache will inflict on impact. Unless stored munitions go off, they usually do not explode.
However, downed aircraft do sometimes start fires. That is especially true on terrain that is primed for it. Salado was dry, with a daily high temperature of 101 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Apache was on a routine training flight when it went down Wednesday. No cause has yet been identified for the crash. The Central Texas Field Office of the Army Criminal Investigation Division is leading the investigation.
